clue.text: Something in chest keeps irregular run in check

indicators.note: a word that keeps something holds it inside, so the check word contains the other piece

parts.note: to stem a flow is to check it

indicators.note: irregular says the letters of run are set out of their usual order

explanation.surface: Someone's heart keeps an erratic beat under control during a jog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'irregular' gives RNU; 'Something in chest' hides a bone, not a treasure box, and 'check' is the verb sense of halting a flow.
explanation.definitionFit: The breastbone is the flat bone at the front of the ribcage, literally something in the chest.

clue.text: What's naughty about the King's Head is too much drink

indicators.note: about means the word for naughty goes around the other letter

parts.note: sinful means wicked or naughty

indicators.note: Head means the first letter of King is taken

explanation.surface: Drinking too much at a pub called the King's Head is wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' gives K, which goes inside SINFUL; the King's Head is a common British pub name.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinful is a British colloquialism for as much alcohol as one can hold, enough to get drunk.

clue.text: Language of neat prose composition

indicators.note: composition implies the letters are put together in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A language suited to tidy prose writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges NEAT PROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is an invented international auxiliary tongue, so it is a language.

clue.text: Is Nick ungodly?

parts.note: ungodly read as not church, with not giving the first part
CH is the abbreviation for church, the godly part being denied

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone named Nick is impious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name, or Old Nick the devil, but it is the definition: a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A notch is a small V-shaped cut, which is exactly what a nick is.

clue.text: Time for military medal

parts.note: the middle of the word summer is MM, the abbreviation for Military Medal

explanation.surface: It is time to award someone a military decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as an instruction, the middle of the word summer, and it gives MM, the Military Medal.
explanation.definitionFit: Midsummer is a point in the year, around the solstice, so it is a time.

clue.text: Little creature goes in to road engineer

indicators.note: one piece goes in, between the letters of the short word to

parts.note: taken as written
an elf is a small mythical being

explanation.surface: A tiny fairy wanders on to a highway being laid by a civil engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Telford was the great Scottish road, bridge and canal engineer, whose name was also given to a new town in Shropshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford was a celebrated Scottish civil engineer famed for roads, bridges and canals.

clue.text: Sharp spasm at sound of shot

indicators.note: at sound of says the word for shot is heard and spelt differently

parts.note: a shot, as in a shot at a target, is a throw

explanation.surface: A sudden pang felt on hearing a gunshot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' suggests gunfire, but here it is a throw, as in having a shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A throe is a violent pang or spasm, as in death throes.

clue.text: Those fail, perhaps, who drop out

indicators.note: perhaps suggests those fail could become something else with the letters reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: People who quit are the ones who fail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges THOSE FAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon belief or give up hope is to drop out of a cause, the idiom here.

clue.text: Cruciform characters for a departed priest

parts.note: OB, for Latin obiit, means died, as on gravestones
Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel

explanation.surface: Cross-shaped symbols to mark a priest who has died.
explanation.walkthrough: Obeli are dagger marks, the cross-shaped symbol used in printing and in old texts, which is why they are called cruciform.
explanation.definitionFit: The obelus or dagger symbol looks like a cross, so these marks are cruciform printed signs.

clue.text: Mother is becoming 20 for compensation

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal
to get older, to age, as one turning twenty does

explanation.surface: A mother hits twenty and receives a payout.
explanation.definitionFit: Damages are money awarded by a court as compensation for loss or injury.

clue.text: Little creature turns to lines, say

parts.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite

indicators.note: turns means the little word to is flipped round to face the other way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A small sprite changes into a set of written lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' makes OT of TO. An impot (short for imposition) is a school punishment of lines to be written out.
explanation.definitionFit: An impot is a school imposition, typically writing lines, so lines are an example of one.

clue.text: Sporty types in pub or South Devon railway?

definitions.meaning: a group who throw arrows at a board in a pub league
the steam railway along the River Dart in Devon

explanation.surface: Are those sporty pub regulars or a heritage railway in South Devon?
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the letters as DART STEAM: the River Dart in South Devon has a steam railway beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub darts team is a squad of players, and Dart steam names a heritage steam line in Devon.

clue.text: Harm of changing custom in rural residence

indicators.note: changing says the letters of harm of are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
use, as in usage, means custom or habit

explanation.surface: Damage caused by altering tradition in a country home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' gives FARMHO; 'custom' is a habit or usage, not a customs duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer's dwelling on agricultural land is a classic countryside residence.

clue.text: Cast pushing the boat out

definitions.meaning: to cast is to throw or hurl
an idiom for a spell of carefree indulgence or spree

explanation.surface: Thrown while celebrating lavishly.
explanation.definitionFit: To fling is to throw, and a fling is a brief bout of self-indulgent enjoyment.

clue.text: Push the boat out without a meal

indicators.note: without means the letter a is taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to launch a boat is literally to push it out into the water

explanation.surface: Getting a vessel afloat with nothing to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'push the boat out' is read literally, not as the idiom for splashing out on a treat.
explanation.definitionFit: The midday meal is a standard everyday meal of the day.

clue.text: Key art ham displayed in theatre

indicators.note: displayed implies the letters are laid out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A key piece of hammy artistry shown on a stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'displayed' rearranges KEY ART HAM. The Theatre Royal Haymarket is a London West End theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Haymarket is a London theatre, the Theatre Royal in the street of that name.

clue.text: Treatment wherewith violent crime is reduced?

definitions.text: Treatment wherewith violent crime is reduced?

indicators.note: violent suggests the word crime is thrown about and its letters disordered

parts.note: taken as written
reduced means made less

explanation.surface: Asks what harsh measures are used to bring down violent offending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'violent' gives MERCI; the whole clue hints at a pitiless crackdown on crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitiless treatment, showing no clemency, is the sort of tough approach used to curb violent offending.

clue.text: Issue a denial over duff I put away

parts.note: re means concerning or over
duff is a pudding, as in plum duff; pud is short for pudding
to put away food is to eat it

explanation.surface: Someone flatly denies having eaten the pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duff' looks like an anagram signal, meaning useless, but here it is the British steamed pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate something is to reject or disown it, which amounts to denying it.

clue.text: Green belt building for composer's private address

indicators.note: building suggests putting the letters together in a new shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Construction on protected countryside to house a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' rearranges GREEN BELT. The composer Engelbert Humperdinck would be called by his first name in private.
explanation.definitionFit: A first name is how intimates privately address someone, and Engelbert was the given name of the composer Humperdinck.

clue.text: Perhaps Labour blunder turns into potential embarrassment …

parts.note: a boob is a silly mistake

indicators.note: turns into tells us the political group word is flipped back to front

parts.note: Labour is an example of a political party

explanation.surface: A Labour gaffe develops into something that could prove awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns into' gives YTRAP; the ellipsis carries the surface on into the next clue about a Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden trap set to catch someone out is a source of possible embarrassment.

clue.text: Boob fashion?

definitions.meaning: ... fashion means in good order, as in shipshape and ... fashion

explanation.surface: A mistake made in the world of style?
explanation.definitionFit: Bristols is rhyming slang for breasts, and Bristol fashion means orderly, as in the nautical phrase.

clue.text: … for Tory old woman rejecting Europe

parts.note: a hag is an ugly old woman

indicators.note: rejecting says the letters for Europe are turned back

parts.note: EU stands for the European Union

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: an elderly Conservative turns her back on Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' turns EU into UE. William Hague was a Conservative party leader; the ellipsis links the surface to the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hague led the Conservative Party, so he is an example of a Tory politician.

clue.text: See about the German student getting on

indicators.note: about means the see word wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city, the seat of a bishop's see
der is a German word for the
L stands for learner or student

explanation.surface: Look at the German scholar making progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a bishop's diocese here, not the verb: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting on is an idiom for growing old, which is what elderly describes.

clue.text: One with business at a foreign resort

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
biz is informal shorthand for business

explanation.surface: Someone who has business dealings at an overseas holiday spot.
explanation.definitionFit: This Balearic island in Spain is a well-known party resort abroad.

clue.text: Former African leader taken up with girl, in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: in a down clue taken up means both pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: Daniel arap Moi was president of Kenya
Di is a short girl's name

explanation.surface: An ex-ruler in Africa goes off with a young woman, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' reverses MOI + DI as a single run. Idi, as in Idi Amin, is the tempting false start, but leaves no sensible remainder.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a characteristic expression, a manner of speaking peculiar to a language.

clue.text: Took the mickey in dire chaos without clear backing

indicators.note: without, meaning outside, puts the jumbled letters around the other piece
chaos signals that the letters of dire are thrown into disorder
backing means the word for clear is read in reverse

parts.note: lucid means clear

explanation.surface: Somebody mocked another for being in a dreadful mess without a clear way back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chaos' gives RIED and 'backing' gives DICUL; 'without' means outside. Taking the mickey is British slang for mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the mickey is a British idiom for teasing or mocking someone, which is what being made fun of means.

clue.text: Determined sport had priority

parts.note: RU is rugby union
led means was in front, had precedence

explanation.surface: The game took precedence, it was decided.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruled, as in a court ruling, means decided or determined.

clue.text: Liberal means of communication?

definitions.meaning: a telegraph wire or message sent by wire

explanation.surface: Is a liberal a channel for passing messages?
explanation.definitionFit: Vince Cable was a Liberal Democrat leader, and a cable is a wire or telegram for sending messages.

clue.text: Man's arms waving, astir like

indicators.note: waving suggests the letters move about and settle in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man flails his arms about in an agitated way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, whose coat of arms is three running legs joined at the hip.
explanation.definitionFit: The three-legged emblem of the Isle of Man is its heraldic arms, so the plural figures are its arms.

clue.text: Hazel, not completely dim

indicators.note: not completely means the surname loses its last letter

parts.note: Hazel Blears was a Labour cabinet minister

explanation.surface: A woman called Hazel who is a bit slow on the uptake.
explanation.walkthrough: Hazel Blears was a British Labour politician; drop her final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Blear as an adjective means dim or blurred, as of sight.

clue.text: Restricted cover for small child's inclusion

indicators.note: inclusion means one piece is enclosed by the cover word

parts.note: a lid is a cover
a mite is a tiny child

explanation.surface: A protective lid limited to keep a youngster safe inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' suggests insurance, but it is simply a lid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something restricted is kept within limits, which is the plain sense of limited.

clue.text: Before court a little lying — straight up!

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: a little means only a small part of lying is kept, its first two letters

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Fibbing a little in front of a judge, followed by an indignant protest of honesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little' keeps just LY of LYING. 'Straight up!' looks like British slang for honestly, but the definition means upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Erectly means in an upright posture, standing vertically, as straight up suggests.
